Napari-OmniEM is a Napari plugin that provides a unified, GPU-accelerated interface for electron microscopy (EM) image processing. Built on top of EM-DINO and OmniEM , it enables scalable, high-quality inference across heterogeneous 2D and 3D EM datasets, bridging foundation models with practical, interactive EM workflows. Installation Getting Started Model Zoo Highlights Napari-OmniEM covers the full workflow, from inference to model management: In-memory inference : tiled, or single-pass Full Volume that avoids sliding-window stitching seams. On-disk (multi-GPU) inference : for volumes too large to fit in memory. Shared backbone across tasks : one ViT-L backbone is cached and reused by every loaded model, keeping GPU memory low. Task-aware model management : add, import, and share your own tasks and models. Tools workbench (🧰) : memory management, weight split/merge, post-processing, and logs in one place. It suits exploratory analysis, large-volume processing, and downstream quantitative studies. Importing Fine-tuned Models You can train your own OmniEM heads with the omniem-train repository and load them into Napari-OmniEM through Add Solution . This page walks through two worked examples from that repository's examples/ folder: EMPIAR-11831 : a 4× super-resolution head ( Image-to-Image ). ME2-Beta : a mitochondria segmentation head ( Image-to-Label ), in 2D and 3D variants. For the general Add Solution reference, see Importing Your Own Models . What training produces After you run a training example ( omniem-train train … infer ), the run's output_dir holds everything you need to import: outputs/<run>/ model.yaml # the model-config file you select in Add Solution weights/ backbone.pt # the shared EM-DINO ViT-L backbone head_best.pt # the trained head (best validation score) head_e<NNN>.pt # per-epoch heads Both examples freeze the backbone ( train.train_encoder: false ), so the backbone is the same EM-DINO ViT-L that Napari-OmniEM already ships as EMDINOv1-ViTL (tag 4246a479 ). That means you import only the head, using the Head-only strategy, and pair it with the existing backbone. If the head-only importer doesn't recognize the backbone Use the Full-scale strategy on the run's combined checkpoint instead, it splits the file into a backbone + head and registers the backbone for you. See Importing Your Own Models . Example 1: 4× super-resolution (Image-to-Image) Source: omniem-train/examples/EMPIAR-11831 (SBF-SEM tobacco tissue). The head restores detail lost to 4× downsampling. Its model.yaml : arch: omniemv1 encoder: emdinov1 img_z: 1 out_channels: 1 # one grayscale map kernel3d_z: null task_type: image2image resize4emdino: true Import it: Open Preferences (⚙️) → Tasks and Models → Solutions and select (or create) an Image-to-Image task. Click Add Solution , then Select model config and pick the run's model.yaml . Choose the Head-only strategy, select weights/head_best.pt , and pair it with EMDINOv1-ViTL . Confirm. The head is copied into the managed weights folder and the solution appears in the task. Use it: run it like any Image-to-Image solution (see In-memory Inference ). This head is trained for 4×, so set the Scale (×) control to 4.0 for its intended factor. Example 2: mitochondria segmentation (Image-to-Label) Source: omniem-train/examples/ME2-Beta (FIB-SEM, part of the MitoEM 2.0 benchmark). The head maps each EM image to a two-class mask, background ( 0 ) and mitochondria ( 1 ). Two configs share the data: Variant img_z kernel3d_z Sample shape 2D ( run_mito_2d ) 1 null 224 × 224 × 1 3D ( run_mito_3d ) 16 3 224 × 224 × 16 The 2D model.yaml : arch: omniemv1 encoder: emdinov1 img_z: 1 out_channels: 2 # background + mitochondria kernel3d_z: null task_type: image2label resize4emdino: false Import it: Select (or create) an Image-to-Label task whose labels are Background and Mitochondria (two labels, matching out_channels: 2 ). Click Add Solution , select the run's model.yaml , choose Head-only , pick weights/head_best.pt , and pair it with EMDINOv1-ViTL . Confirm. Repeat with the 3D run's model.yaml + head_best.pt to add the 3D variant as a second solution (it needs z ≥ 16 ). Use it: run it like any Image-to-Label solution. The output is a mask with the Background / Mitochondria labels. After importing Imported solutions behave exactly like the built-ins: they appear in the Task / Solution menus for in-memory and local inference, and you can export or share them. To manage the shared backbone they run on, see Backbones . References Wickramanayake, J. S., & Czymmek, K. J. (2023). A conventional fixation volume electron microscopy protocol for plants. Methods in Cell Biology, 177 , 83-99. Liu, P. (2026). MitoEM 2.0: A Benchmark for Challenging 3D Mitochondria Instance Segmentation from EM Images [Dataset]. Zenodo.

docs.text: Multi-Task Inference: Super-Resolution + Segmentation Screenshots Screenshots on this page show the v0.2 interface and are pending update. One advantage of Napari-OmniEM is the ability to chain multiple models for analysis. This page demonstrates how applying super-resolution before segmentation can yield better mitochondria segmentation results compared to direct segmentation on the original data (Figure 5 in the manuscript). The experiment uses the downsampled glycolytic muscle EM dataset from MitoLab . The downsampled data is available as sample data in Napari-OmniEM. This page walks through two workflows: Direct segmentation : segment mitochondria directly in the downsampled data. Super-resolution + segmentation : upsample the data first, then segment. Data Click File → Open Sample → OmniEM → EM to load the bundled sample data (this loads three datasets; use the GlyMuscle (3D) layer here). Open the OmniEM panel and select the data in the Data dropdown. Set the z-dimension to 0 . Then open the Image Properties panel to verify the data size: [302, 168, 336] . Direct Mitochondria Segmentation Select Mitochondria Segmentation in the Task dropdown. We recommend the ViT-L-2D solution for its better generalization. Adjust the hyperparameters as needed, for example, set the output name to raw-seg to identify the result, and reduce the batch size to 1 to reduce memory usage. Click Run model and wait for the results. Super-Resolution Select Super-resolution in the Task dropdown. Set the Scale (×) control to 2.0 , this doubles both in-plane axes (168 → 336 and 336 → 672); the z-axis is never scaled. The panel shows the resulting output shape. Click Run model to start super-resolution inference. After inference completes, we recommend removing unused data layers and switching to Grid view mode to compare results side by side. Mitochondria Segmentation on Super-Resolved Data Select the new super-resolution image in the Data dropdown (layers sync automatically; use 🔄 Synchronize Data only if it is missing). Select Mitochondria Segmentation as the task. For better results, increase the XY Input size to a larger value (e.g., 448 ) to better fit the increased data resolution. Click Run model and wait for the segmentation results. Switch to 3D view mode to see the differences more clearly. Conclusion Napari-OmniEM enables flexible chaining of multiple models within a single interactive workflow. By combining tasks such as super-resolution and segmentation, users can leverage complementary models to achieve better analysis outcomes than any single model alone. This composability is a core strength of the plugin, making it adaptable to diverse EM datasets and analysis goals. docs.text: Model Zoo All models in Napari-OmniEM share the same core architecture: OmniEM . OmniEM Architecture OmniEM is a unified framework designed to support multiple electron microscopy (EM) tasks within a consistent architectural paradigm. Model behavior is determined by: Task type Input dimensionality configuration Shared backbone, per-task heads Every model reuses one shared ViT-L backbone : the EM-DINO encoder (tag 4246a479 , shown in the GUI as EMDINOv1-ViTL ), plus a small per-task head . The backbone is loaded once and borrowed by every task that uses it, so running several models together does not reload the encoder and keeps GPU memory low. Weights are stored in a managed folder as one shared backbone_<tag>.pt plus a head_*.pt per solution. See Backbones and Importing Your Own Models . Task Types Models are grouped by the GUI Task Type : Image-to-Image : the output is an image of the same kind as the input (e.g. super-resolution, denoising). Image-to-Label : the output is a labeled mask (e.g. mitochondria). Dimensionality Support OmniEM models can operate in either 2D or 3D mode. 2D Models img_z = 1 Accept: 2D input 3D input (automatically reshaped into slice-wise 2D inference) 3D reshaping can be disabled by the user if inter-slice consistency is a concern. 3D Models img_z > 1 Accept: 3D input only Require minimum Z-dimension ≥ img_z No 2D inference allowed Data Type Configuration The datatypes field defines acceptable input dimensionality: 2D data 3D data Available Models Image-to-Image Super-resolution Denoise Image-to-Label Mitochondria Segmentation (2D & 3D variants) Training and Fine-tuning OmniEM If you would like to train or fine-tune OmniEM on your own dataset, please refer to the official training repository. 👉 The training repository will be publicly released soon. Note: Models trained externally must export compatible weight files and configuration metadata to be imported into Napari-OmniEM.

docs.text: Mitochondria Segmentation Task Type Image-to-Label Overview The Mitochondria Segmentation model performs pixel-wise classification of mitochondria in electron microscopy (EM) images. It supports both 2D slice-wise model (trained on CEM-Mitolab dataset ) and 3D volumetric-input model (trained on MitoEM dataset ). This task outputs a labeled mask with the following classes: Background Mitochondria Available Solutions 1. ViT-L-2D Configuration The task heads run on the shared 4246a479 backbone ( EMDINOv1-ViTL ): - name: ViT-L-2D datatypes: [2, 3] img_z: 1 weights_head: head_mito-seg-ViT-L-2D.pt backbone_tag: 4246a479 head_tag: 7c18ec1e Characteristics img_z = 1 (2D model) Accepts: 2D input 3D input (processed slice-wise) No inter-slice fusion Suitable for fast inference and datasets without strong Z-continuity Recommended Use Cases 2D EM slice segmentation Large-scale screening When Z-alignment consistency is uncertain 2. docs.text: Importing Your Own Models Napari-OmniEM ships with built-in tasks, but you can add your own fine-tuned OmniEM models to any task through Preferences → Tasks and Models → Add Solution . Every model is stored as a small task head on top of a shared backbone (see Backbones below). When you import a model you tell the plugin which backbone it belongs to and which head to use; the plugin copies the head into its managed weights folder and records it. Before you start A model-config file ( .yaml ) that describes the model (architecture, task type, number of output labels, normalization statistics). Use the config that was shipped alongside the weights : see the warning below. A weights file ( .pt ), either a full checkpoint (backbone + head in one file) or a head-only file that was split from one. Match the config to the weights A model-config .yaml is not cryptographically tied to a checkpoint; nothing stops you pairing the wrong two. Always use the config file that was distributed with those weights. A mismatched config passes the file checks but produces wrong results or fails when the model loads. Add a solution Open Preferences (⚙️) → Tasks and Models → Solutions , select the task the model belongs to, and click Add Solution . Select the model config (.yaml). Its contents appear read-only so you can confirm the architecture, task type, label count, and normalization. Choose an import strategy : Full-scale (.pt) : a complete checkpoint. On import the plugin splits it into the shared backbone plus a task head. If a matching backbone is already registered, only the new head is kept and the existing backbone is reused; if the backbone is new, you are offered a chance to name it. Head-only (split .pt) : a head file produced by a previous split. This option is available only when a matching backbone is already registered (the head needs a donor backbone to run). Pick the weights file, then confirm. The head is copied into the managed weights folder as head_<task>-<solution>.pt . If the import is rejected The plugin validates the model before writing anything, so a rejected import leaves no files behind. Common messages and what they mean: Message Meaning Unsupported model / encoder The config's architecture is not one this build supports. Task type mismatch The config's task type doesn't match the task you're adding to (Image-to-Image vs Image-to-Label). Label count mismatch An Image-to-Label config declares a different number of labels than the task. Backbone / encoder mismatch The head was trained for a different backbone than the one selected. Sharing and exporting Once a solution works you can package it for someone else, or repackage its weights: Export Weights (Solutions tab) writes this solution's weights out as either a Combined single .pt or a Split pair (backbone + head). Combined files load anywhere; split pairs are smaller to share when the recipient already has the backbone. Dump Task / Import Task move a whole task (all its solutions) between installs. See Task & Solution Management for the full sharing workflow. Note that Dump writes the task description only ; the weights are exported separately and must sit in the folder you point Import at. The File Management tool (🧰 → File Management) can split a combined checkpoint or merge a backbone + head back into one file without adding a solution. See Tools Workbench . Backbones Every model runs on a shared backbone : one large ViT-L encoder (EM-DINO, shown as EMDINOv1-ViTL ). The backbone is loaded once and borrowed by every task that uses it, so keeping several models ready does not reload the encoder and keeps GPU memory low. Backbones are managed under Preferences (⚙️) → Tasks and Models → Backbones . The backbone inventory The Backbones table lists one row per registered backbone: Column Meaning Display Name Friendly name (defaults to the tag). Tag Short content fingerprint that identifies the weights. Arch Encoder architecture (e.g. emdinov1 ). Solutions How many task heads currently reference this backbone. Actions Rename and Remove for this backbone. The built-in backbone ( 4246a479 , EMDINOv1-ViTL ) is always present and its Remove action is disabled. Add a backbone Click + Add Backbone . There are two ways to add one: Register split .pt : point at a standalone backbone file (already split out of a checkpoint). It is copied into the managed weights folder and registered. Extract from combined .pt : point at a full checkpoint; the backbone part is extracted, stored, and registered, leaving the original file untouched. Rename changes only the display name (up to 64 characters); the tag never changes. Remove a backbone Selecting Remove does different things depending on the backbone, and it never silently deletes something another model needs: Built-in backbone : cannot be removed. In use : if any model is currently loaded on it, or any solution references it, removal is blocked. Unload the models (🧰 → Memory Management → Remove) or remove/reassign the solutions first. External file (stored outside the managed weights folder): removed from the registry only; the physical file is left where it is. Managed file (inside the weights folder, unreferenced): you are asked whether to also delete the file or just deregister it. Two different “remove”s Preferences → Backbones → Remove takes a backbone out of the registry (and optionally deletes its file). 🧰 → Memory Management → Remove backbone only frees it from memory for this session; it stays registered. See Tools Workbench . Backbone settings The weights storage folder and the backbone cache size are set in Preferences → Settings → General settings ; see the Preferences reference . Weights storage folder : where the plugin keeps backbone_<tag>.pt and head_*.pt . Changing it offers to move the existing managed files to the new location. Backbone cache size : how many distinct backbones may stay resident at once. Sharing one backbone across tasks is what keeps multi-task GPU use low.

docs.text: Inference Napari-OmniEM offers two ways to run a model: In-memory (main panel): the quickest way to run a model, best for interactive exploration and small-to-medium data that fits in memory. Local (on-disk) (📁 wizard): streams large volumes from disk with bounded memory and multi-GPU support. Task and solution selection and the sliding-window parameters are the same in both. Memory and scratch-disk guidance for either mode is in Tips & common pitfalls below. In-memory inference In-memory inference runs directly in the main Napari-OmniEM panel on data loaded as napari image layers. It is the quickest way to run a model and is best for interactive exploration, debugging, and small-to-medium EM datasets . Everything stays in memory The input volume, the intermediate tiles, and the result all live in GPU/CPU memory at once, so this mode is bounded by how much memory you have. For volumes too large to hold in memory, use Local inference instead. You can run in one of two modes : Sliding window (default): the volume is split into overlapping tiles, each is run through the model, and the tiles are stitched back together. Uses less GPU memory and handles larger inputs. Full Volume : the whole image is fed to the model in a single forward pass. Avoids stitching seams but needs more GPU memory. See Full Volume mode below. Select data Load image data into napari via File → Open File(s) . The data will appear as one or more image layers . Loaded layers are detected automatically. If one is missing (rarely), click 🔄 Synchronize Data to rescan. Select the target image from the Data dropdown list. If the selected data is a 3D volume , specify the z-dimension : By default, the axis with the minimum side length is automatically chosen. You can override this if your data uses a different axis convention. Select task and solution Choose a Task corresponding to the intended processing goal, an Image-to-Image task (e.g. denoising, super-resolution) or an Image-to-Label task (e.g. mitochondria segmentation). Select a compatible Solution from the Solution list. The list is filtered automatically by the selected data: only solutions whose dimensionality and modality match the chosen layer appear, so you cannot pick a model that does not fit your data. Not sure which to choose? Click the 💡 button next to the Task or Solution dropdown to show its details. For fuller descriptions of the built-in models, see the Model Zoo . Terminology note - Task : defines what problem is being solved. - Solution : a concrete model + configuration that solves a task. This terminology is consistent across in-memory and local inference. Output options by task type The panel shows different output controls depending on the task type: Image-to-Image : a single Scale (×) control (range 1.0–8.0, step 0.5). The ratio is applied to the in-plane (X/Y) axes together; the Z axis is never scaled. 1.0 keeps the size; restoration never downscales. The panel shows the resulting output shape live. (Some models are trained for modest scaling, the super-resolution model recommends staying below 3.0× .) Image-to-Label : a read-only table of the label → value mapping that the output mask will use. Nothing to set here. Advanced settings The Advanced section holds per-run overrides. Defaults come from Preferences ; if unsure, the defaults are safe for a first run. Full Volume : switches to Full Volume mode; see the next section . Sliding-window only (these grey out under Full Volume): Overlap , Batch Size , XY Input Size : tiling controls; see Sliding Window Parameters . Blend mode : how overlapping tiles are combined ( constant or gaussian ). Both modes: Normalization source : scan-data (statistics measured over the whole volume) or model (the model's built-in statistics). Full Volume mode Tick Full Volume to feed the whole image to the model in a single forward pass instead of tiling. This avoids sliding-window stitching seams and works for both Image-to-Image and Image-to-Label tasks, but it uses more GPU memory. The sliding-window controls (overlap, batch, XY, blend) grey out; the normalization selector still applies. If the input is not square, you'll be asked to run at the height or the width as the square size; the original aspect ratio is restored and output-scaled afterward, the image is not cropped. Full Volume with the 3D mitochondria model The ViT-L-3D model may produce boundary gaps between blocks under Full Volume; prefer sliding-window mode for it. See the model card . Run inference Click Run model to open the inference dialog. It shows the device, the work to be done (batch count or the padded input/output shape), and the estimated GPU memory range for the run. Start the run from the dialog. When it finishes, the OK button becomes Redo so you can re-run with changed settings; the result appears in napari as a new layer. For Image-to-Image results, you can rescale output intensity back to the input's range with the Post-process → Image-to-Image tool. Local (on-disk) inference Local (on-disk) inference is activated by clicking the 📁 button in the main Napari-OmniEM panel. Data are loaded from local files using dask.array , and intermediate results are stored as temporary HDF5 files (more efficient backends are planned). It is a step-by-step wizard: Input Data → Task → Advanced settings → Run → Output. Open the panel Click the 📁 icon in the main Napari-OmniEM panel. This option is enabled only when a compatible GPU is available. Step 1: Select data Click Browse File to select a local image or volume. Common image formats read by dask-image are supported, such as TIFF (including multi-page stacks, which load as a 3D volume), PNG , and JPEG . The data must be 2D (H, W) , 3D (Z, H, W) , or a colour variant (H, W, C) / (Z, H, W, C) ; other shapes are rejected. The model works on single-channel data. If you load a colour or multi-channel image, a Channel selector appears so you can reduce it to one channel: Convert to grayscale (weighted) (default): combine the colour channels into one grayscale channel. Extract single channel : keep one channel, chosen by its 0-based index . If the data are 3D, specify the z-dimension : By default, the axis with the minimum side length is selected. Override this if your data use a different axis convention. Everything streams from disk Every input (2D, colour, or 3D) is processed as a streamed 3D volume with bounded memory, so even large 2D images run here without loading whole. Step 2: Select task and solution Task and solution selection is the same as in in-memory inference. Only solutions compatible with the selected data will be shown. docs.text: In-memory inference runs directly in the main Napari-OmniEM panel on data loaded as napari image layers. It is the quickest way to run a model and is best for interactive exploration, debugging, and small-to-medium EM datasets . Everything stays in memory The input volume, the intermediate tiles, and the result all live in GPU/CPU memory at once, so this mode is bounded by how much memory you have. For volumes too large to hold in memory, use Local inference instead. You can run in one of two modes : Sliding window (default): the volume is split into overlapping tiles, each is run through the model, and the tiles are stitched back together. Uses less GPU memory and handles larger inputs. Full Volume : the whole image is fed to the model in a single forward pass. Avoids stitching seams but needs more GPU memory. See Full Volume mode below.

docs.text: Installation Napari-OmniEM is installed from source: clone the repository, create an environment, install the plugin, then download the pre-trained weights. 1. Clone the repository The code, configs, and example data are on GitHub: git clone https://github.com/pku-maleilab/napari-omniem.git cd napari-omniem 2. Create the environment and install the plugin Run these from the repository root (the napari-omniem/ directory you just cloned into): # Create a new conda environment (Python 3.11 required) conda create -n napari-omniem python=3.11 conda activate napari-omniem # Install PyTorch first. Choose the command for your platform (CUDA version # or CPU) from the official selector: https://pytorch.org/get-started/locally/ # Example (CUDA 11.8): pip install torch torchvision torchaudio --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu118 # CPU-only alternative: # pip install torch torchvision torchaudio # Install the plugin in editable mode from the repository root. # Editable mode is required: the plugin loads weights from the # weights_split/ folder relative to the cloned repository (step 3). # This also pulls omniem from PyPI (a normal dependency). pip install -e . 3. Download the pre-trained weights The model weights are distributed separately. Download the weights_split folder from Google Drive . Place its contents into a weights_split/ folder at the root of the cloned repository , so the layout is: napari-omniem/ # the cloned repository root ├── pyproject.toml # (already present) editable-install target ├── README.md # (already present) ├── src/ # (already present) the plugin source └── weights_split/ # (you create this) place the downloaded files here ├── backbone_4246a479.pt # shared ViT-L backbone (~1.2 GB) ├── head_denoise-emdiffuse-l.pt ├── head_superreso-emdiffuse-l.pt ├── head_mito-seg-ViT-L-2D.pt └── head_mito-seg-ViT-L-3D.pt weights_split/ sits next to pyproject.toml , src/ , and README.md at the repository root, not inside src/ . If those files are its siblings, it is in the right place. You can change this folder later from Preferences → Settings → Weights storage folder : saving a new location offers to move your existing managed weights there. See the Preferences reference and Backbones . 4. Launch napari Once napari is running, open Plugins and select OmniEM . Troubleshooting PyQt6 conflict. This plugin uses PyQt5. If PyQt6 was pulled into the environment by a previous install and napari fails to start with a Qt binding error, remove it and reinstall: pip uninstall -y PyQt6 PyQt6-Qt6 PyQt6-sip || true Linux / Wayland. If the napari window fails to open (blank window or an xcb /OpenGL platform error), pin the Qt platform once for this environment, then plain napari works: conda env config vars set QT_API=pyqt5 QT_QPA_PLATFORM=xcb PYOPENGL_PLATFORM=glx conda activate napari-omniem # re-activate to apply Notes Ensure your GPU drivers and CUDA runtime are installed before installing PyTorch with CUDA support. Large-volume inference needs sufficient GPU memory and disk space. Multi-GPU inference is supported when multiple CUDA devices are available.

docs.text: Task & Solution Management Napari-OmniEM lets you manage tasks and solutions (models + configurations) from the GUI. Open ⚙️ Preferences → Tasks and Models → Solutions . Screenshots Some screenshots on this page show the v0.2 interface and are pending update. Concepts A Task defines the problem type, Image-to-Image (e.g. denoising, super-resolution) or Image-to-Label (e.g. mitochondria segmentation). A Solution is a concrete model + configuration that solves a task. A task may hold several solutions; each solution belongs to exactly one task. Adding your own solutions and managing shared backbones has its own page: Importing Your Own Models : the Add Solution flow and the shared backbones behind every model. Managing tasks New Task Click New Task and provide: Task Type : Image-to-Image or Image-to-Label . Full Name : the name shown in the GUI selection menus (must be unique). Short Name : a concise identifier used to store the task's config file (must be unique). For an Image-to-Label task, also define each output label and its meaning; each label is one output class of the model. Enable / Disable Task Select a task, then use Enable Task / Disable Task (only the applicable one is active). A disabled task does not appear in the in-memory or local inference menus; its solutions stay stored and return when you re-enable it. Delete Task Delete Task removes a task and its config permanently. If the task's solutions have head files inside the managed weights folder, you're asked whether to delete those files too or keep them. The shared backbone is never deleted here. Dump Task / Import Task (sharing) Move a whole task between installs: Dump Task writes the task description only : a .yaml listing its solutions. It does not copy weights. Import Task reads such a .yaml back and registers the task under a unique short name you provide, pointing it at a folder that holds the weight files. Because Dump writes only the description, sharing a task means sending both the dumped YAML and the weight files: Dump Task → get mytask.yaml . Export Weights for each solution (see Importing Your Own Models ) into a folder. Send the YAML + the weights folder. The recipient uses Import Task , selects the YAML, points at the weights folder, and gives a unique short name. Head files must match the YAML Every solution's head file must be present in the selected weights folder and its filename must match the one recorded in the dumped YAML. If you renamed a Split export, update the YAML (or re-export) so the names line up, otherwise the import can't find the weights. Managing solutions Add Solution Click Add Solution to import a fine-tuned OmniEM model into the selected task. The full flow, model-config file, full-scale vs head-only strategy, and what the validation messages mean, is documented in Importing Your Own Models . Solution metadata cannot be changed after a solution is added; to change it, remove the solution and add it again. Remove Solution Select a solution and click Remove Solution . If the solution's head file lives in the managed weights folder, you're offered a choice: delete the file too , keep it , or cancel . Removing a solution deletes it from the task config; a shared backbone is never removed by this action. Export Weights Export Weights writes a solution's weights out as a Combined single .pt or a Split pair (backbone + head); see Importing Your Own Models . Best practices Use descriptive task and solution names. Dump a task (and export its weights) before major changes. Keep your weights in the managed weights storage folder so the plugin can find and move them for you.

docs.text: Preferences reference The ⚙️ Preferences button opens the settings dialog. It has two tabs: Settings (defaults and software-wide options, described here) and Tasks and Models (see Task & Solution Management , Importing Your Own Models , and Backbones ). Changes here need no restart (new tasks do, that is noted where it applies). Inference defaults These set the starting values for every run; you can still override them per run in the Advanced settings (in-memory) or wizard (on-disk). Setting Notes Device Default compute device ( cpu or cuda:N ). Batch size Tiles processed together. Default 4 . XY input size Square tile size fed to the model. Default 224 (range 112–896, step 112). Overlap Fractional overlap between tiles. Default 0.25 . Blend mode How overlapping tiles are combined, constant or gaussian . Normalization source scan-data (whole-volume statistics) or model (the model's built-in statistics). See Sliding window parameters below for what each of the tiling parameters does. Sliding window parameters Sliding-window inference tiles a large image into overlapping windows, runs each through the model, and merges the results. It is used by both in-memory (tiled) and on-disk inference. The values above are the defaults; each has a per-run override (the Advanced section in-memory, or the wizard on-disk). Input XY size Spatial size (in pixels) of each window in the XY plane. Larger windows give more context and usually better quality; smaller windows use less GPU memory but can weaken boundary consistency. Default 224 ; range 112–896 in steps of 112 . Use the largest size that fits in GPU memory. Batch size Number of windows processed together in one forward pass. Larger batches raise throughput; smaller batches use less GPU memory. Default 4 ; set 1 when GPU memory is limited and increase gradually. Overlap Fractional overlap between adjacent windows ( 0.0 to 0.5 ). Higher overlap smooths boundaries and reduces stitching artifacts but is slower. Default 0.25 ; lower it toward 0.1 for speed on tolerant Image-to-Image runs, and keep it higher for boundary-sensitive Image-to-Label tasks. Blend mode How overlapping tiles are combined when merged: constant (uniform) or gaussian (weighted toward tile centers, smoother seams). Practical tips Prefer larger XY sizes over larger batch sizes for better quality. Keep overlap ≥ 0.1 to avoid visible stitching artifacts. On out-of-memory (OOM) errors, reduce batch size, then XY size, then overlap (last resort). See Inference Tips & Common Pitfalls for memory usage, out-of-memory recovery, and scratch-disk guidance. General settings Software-wide options. Weights storage folder Where the plugin keeps its managed weight files ( backbone_<tag>.pt and head_*.pt ). Use Browse… to change it; the plugin offers to move the existing managed files to the new folder so your models keep working. Backbone cache size How many distinct shared backbones may stay resident in memory at once. Because tasks share a backbone, a small cache is usually enough; raise it only if you switch between models that use different backbones. GPU and CPU memory limits Two rows, GPU (VRAM) limit and CPU (RAM) limit : let you cap how much a run may use. Each row has: A source: Auto (half of the device's total memory), Custom (the MB value in the spinbox), or Off (no limit). A mode: Hard or Soft . Hard blocks a run when its upper-end memory estimate exceeds the cap; Soft only warns and lets you continue. “Proceed anyway” Before a run, the plugin estimates the memory it needs. If that estimate can't be guaranteed, because it exceeds a soft limit or because the actual free GPU memory or scratch disk is short, you'll see a Proceed anyway option. It lets you run at your own risk; the run may still hit an out-of-memory error. Buttons at the bottom Save or Reset all controls, and Close the dialog.

docs.text: Sliding-window inference tiles a large image into overlapping windows, runs each through the model, and merges the results. It is used by both in-memory (tiled) and on-disk inference. The values above are the defaults; each has a per-run override (the Advanced section in-memory, or the wizard on-disk).
docs.title: Sliding window parameters

docs.text: Spatial size (in pixels) of each window in the XY plane. Larger windows give more context and usually better quality; smaller windows use less GPU memory but can weaken boundary consistency. Default 224 ; range 112–896 in steps of 112 . Use the largest size that fits in GPU memory.
docs.title: Input XY size

docs.text: Number of windows processed together in one forward pass. Larger batches raise throughput; smaller batches use less GPU memory. Default 4 ; set 1 when GPU memory is limited and increase gradually.
docs.title: Batch size

docs.text: Fractional overlap between adjacent windows ( 0.0 to 0.5 ). Higher overlap smooths boundaries and reduces stitching artifacts but is slower. Default 0.25 ; lower it toward 0.1 for speed on tolerant Image-to-Image runs, and keep it higher for boundary-sensitive Image-to-Label tasks.
docs.title: Overlap

docs.text: How overlapping tiles are combined when merged: constant (uniform) or gaussian (weighted toward tile centers, smoother seams).
docs.title: Blend mode

docs.text: Prefer larger XY sizes over larger batch sizes for better quality. Keep overlap ≥ 0.1 to avoid visible stitching artifacts. On out-of-memory (OOM) errors, reduce batch size, then XY size, then overlap (last resort). See Inference Tips & Common Pitfalls for memory usage, out-of-memory recovery, and scratch-disk guidance.

docs.text: Tools Workbench (🧰) The 🧰 More Tools button on the OmniEM toolbar opens a workbench of utilities that sit alongside the main inference panel. It has six tabs. Memory Management Load, measure, and free models, and watch live GPU/host memory. A readout shows which backbone is resident and its reference count, which heads are loaded, and current GPU allocated / reserved / free and host RAM. Each action reports how much memory it freed. Button What it does Preload Load the selected solution now so the first run is fast. Profile this solution Measure this solution's real memory use. Not a passive inspection : it may evict currently loaded models and run GPU forward passes to take the measurement. Remove Unload the selected solution's head from memory. Remove backbone Free a shared backbone from memory (only when nothing references it). It stays registered; see Backbones . Clear all models Unload every head and backbone. Clear temporal data Delete on-disk inference scratch files (see the warning below). Refresh Update the memory readout. Clear temporal data affects open results On-disk inference results stay backed by their scratch file while you view them. Clear temporal data deletes those files immediately, which can make still-open result layers unreadable. Save anything you need first. File Management Split a combined checkpoint into a backbone + head pair, or merge a backbone and a head back into one combined file, without adding a solution. Useful for preparing weights to share. See also Importing Your Own Models . Pre-process Reserved for input pre-processing tools. Coming soon. Post-process Image-to-Image : rescale a model output's intensity back to the input's range. Pick the original image (the intensity reference) and the model output; optionally replace the output layer in place. This is the recommended finishing step after an Image-to-Image run. Image-to-Label : reserved for label post-processing. Coming soon. Logs View the plugin log without leaving napari. Filter by number of lines, by date, and by keyword; Clear Log empties the log file after confirmation. More Documentation and project links, and how to cite the work.
